passage:
For months Francis had carried the year he left college and told his parents it was a transfer. He wanted Yogesh to know, and he was afraid Yogesh would see him differently. So he began small, on a walk. "I wasn't very good at the job I had at twenty. I quit before they could fire me." Yogesh only nodded and said, "That sounds like a hard time." Nothing changed in his face, and Francis felt his shoulders drop a little.

Three weeks later, on the balcony, he took a breath. "There's something else. I never transferred. I dropped out, and I've been ashamed of it since." His voice shook on the last word.

Yogesh felt honoured and completely unsure what to say. His mind offered him solutions, a phone call to the college, a plan, and he set them all aside. He put a hand on the railing next to Francis's and said, "Thank you for telling me. I'm glad you did." He did not ask why. He did not fix it.

Next week Gurpreet asked casually over tea, "What's up with Francis lately? He seems lighter." Yogesh smiled and stirred his cup. "He's doing better. That's all I'll say."

qa.q: What did Francis tell his parents about leaving college?
qa.a: He told them it was a transfer.

qa.q: How did Francis's small first disclosure and Yogesh's quiet reactions connect to the bigger conversation on the balcony?
qa.a: Francis began small on a walk and saw Yogesh nod kindly, so on the balcony he told him he had dropped out. Yogesh said thank you, did not fix it, and told Gurpreet only that Francis was doing better.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Francis said he had dropped out?
qa.a: He felt honoured and unsure what to say, so he set aside his urge to offer solutions.

qa.q: What could Francis do if he wants to share another old shame with Yogesh later?
qa.a: He could share it at his own pace, a little at a time, and keep noticing whether Yogesh holds it with care.

grounding: A partner's slow confession of an old shame is seen from the person who fears judgment and the person who listens and keeps the confidence.
